desc: Fuses traditional English ballads with electric rock, featuring Sandy Denny and Dave Swarbrick's fiddle.
Ambitious double album of orchestral ballads and country-tinged songs with lush strings.
Fractured, polyrhythmic blues and free-jazz collisions, produced by Frank Zappa.
Horn-driven jazz rock fronted by David Clayton-Thomas, including Spinning Wheel and You've Made Me So Very Happy.
Gram Parsons and Chris Hillman blend honky-tonk, soul and psychedelia with fuzzed pedal steel.
Jesse Colin Young-led folk rock with jazzy touches, made after the band moved to Northern California.
Norman Whitfield steers the Temptations into psychedelic soul with wah-wah guitar and social commentary.
Scott Walker's first album of all self-written songs, orchestral and literate, released under his birth name.
Sly Stone's band mixes funk, rock and gospel, including Everyday People and I Want to Take You Higher.
Primal, repetitive proto-punk produced by John Cale, with wah-drenched riffs and Iggy Pop's sneer.
Extended live improvisations from San Francisco shows, anchored by a 23-minute Dark Star.
Ray Davies' concept album about postwar English working-class life, written for an unmade TV play.
Live prison concert with a raucous inmate audience, featuring the hit A Boy Named Sue.
Debut built on close three-part harmonies and acoustic guitar, opening with Suite: Judy Blue Eyes.
Hushed debut of fingerpicked guitar and Robert Kirby string arrangements, produced by Joe Boyd.
Tim Buckley's turn toward jazz, with long, loose songs built on vibraphone, upright bass and soaring vocals.
Four long tracks, including an 18-minute By the Time I Get to Phoenix with spoken intro.
Mostly instrumental jazz rock with extended guitar solos, plus Captain Beefheart singing on Willie the Pimp.
Debut recorded live at Detroit's Grande Ballroom, a raw, politically charged blast of high-volume rock.
Rolling Stones album bookended by Gimme Shelter and You Can't Always Get What You Want.
Skip Spence's solo album, recorded alone in Nashville after leaving Moby Grape, playing every instrument.
Quieter, gentler record after John Cale's departure, featuring Pale Blue Eyes and Candy Says.
Sandy Denny-led folk rock including Who Knows Where the Time Goes and an epic A Sailor's Life.
Pete Townshend's double-album rock opera about a deaf, dumb and blind boy who becomes a messiah.
Rustic, ensemble-driven songs evoking rural American history, including The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down.
Double-album debut of horn-powered jazz rock, including Beginnings and Terry Kath's Free Form Guitar.
First album with Crazy Horse, featuring long ragged guitar jams like Down by the River.
Two long, hushed electric pieces assembled by Teo Macero, foreshadowing jazz fusion and ambient music.
Sparse, Nashville-recorded second album produced by Bob Johnston, including Bird on the Wire and Story of Isaac.
Heavy, riff-driven album recorded on tour, opening with Whole Lotta Love and featuring Moby Dick.
The Beatles' last recorded album, with a side-two medley and songs including Something and Here Comes the Sun.
Swamp-blues-inspired rock from California, featuring Proud Mary and the extended Keep On Chooglin'.
Tight, rootsy album with Bad Moon Rising and the title track, recalling rural childhood imagery.
Debut defining progressive rock with mellotron washes, jazz-inflected aggression and 21st Century Schizoid Man.
Debut blending heavy blues and folk, with Jimmy Page's riffs and John Bonham's thunderous drumming.
Stark, emotionally raw solo album shaped by primal therapy, with spare drums, bass and piano.
Syd Barrett's fragile first solo album, produced partly by Roger Waters and David Gilmour.
Rod Stewart's second solo album, mixing folk, soul and rock with members of the Faces.
Van Morrison blends jazz, soul and folk with horns, including the title track and Into the Mystic.
Soft pop led by Karen Carpenter's warm alto, featuring the Bacharach title track and We've Only Just Begun.
Polished, eclectic psychedelic rock produced by David Briggs, including Nature's Way and Mr. Skin.
Eric Clapton's double album of unrequited love, with Duane Allman's slide guitar on the title track.
Ferocious live set from Leeds University, featuring extended versions of My Generation and Summertime Blues.
Gentle, acoustic singer-songwriter album featuring Fire and Rain and the title lullaby.
Double album of four side-long pieces blending jazz, rock and tape experimentation.
Solo debut featuring Love the One You're With, with guest guitar from Jimi Hendrix and Eric Clapton.
Latin percussion meets blues-rock guitar on Black Magic Woman and Oye Como Va.
Harmony-rich acoustic Americana, featuring Truckin', Ripple and Box of Rain.
Sitar meets Moog and rock rhythms, including instrumental covers of Jumpin' Jack Flash and Light My Fire.
Raw, near-live recording with Steve Mackay's free saxophone pushing the Stooges into frenzied noise.
Homemade solo debut, largely recorded alone at home, including Maybe I'm Amazed.
Acoustic folk pop featuring Wild World and Father and Son, produced by Paul Samwell-Smith.
Triple album co-produced with Phil Spector, including My Sweet Lord and extended jams.
Final Simon and Garfunkel album, featuring the gospel-styled title ballad and The Boxer.
First Mark II album, pairing Jon Lord's distorted organ and Ritchie Blackmore's guitar, including Child in Time.
First album with Neil Young, including Teach Your Children, Our House and a cover of Woodstock.
Steve Winwood-led blend of jazz, rock and English folk, with a traditional title song.
A return to harder blues rock, including Roadhouse Blues and Peace Frog.
Mix of fragile piano ballads and guitar rock, including Southern Man and Only Love Can Break Your Heart.
Sprawling double album of electric improvisation, heavily edited by Teo Macero from studio jams.
Debut that helped define heavy metal, opening with tolling bells and a tritone riff.
Hit-packed album with Up Around the Bend, Lookin' Out My Back Door and an 11-minute Grapevine.
Largely acoustic, folk-inspired album partly written at Bron-Yr-Aur, opening with Immigrant Song.
Includes War Pigs, Iron Man and the title track, cementing Sabbath's heavy, doom-laden sound.
Debut of character-driven story songs, including Sam Stone, Angel from Montgomery and Hello in There.
Rod Stewart's breakthrough, featuring Maggie May and a mix of folk, rock and soul covers.
Stripped-down, Stones-style rock and roll from the San Francisco band.
Murky, sparse funk using an early drum machine, including Family Affair, reflecting Sly Stone's darker turn.
Bee Gees album of lush ballads, including How Can You Mend a Broken Heart.
Known for the eight-minute title song and Vincent, a tribute to Van Gogh.
Loose, good-time rock and roll featuring Stay With Me, with Rod Stewart and Ronnie Wood.
Dolly Parton's autobiographical album, led by the title song about her childhood poverty.
Hazy folk with wordless harmonies, recorded with members of the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane.
Live recording with Ginger Baker drumming alongside Africa '70, stretching afrobeat grooves across long jams.
Soundtrack to the 1971 film, known for its wah-wah guitar and hi-hat theme.
Live double album of extended jams, with Duane Allman's slide guitar and Whipping Post.
Introspective, ecology-minded album featuring Til I Die and the Smile-era title track.
Piano-led songs including It's Too Late and You've Got a Friend; a major 1970s bestseller.
Side-long title suite of keyboard-driven prog about a mechanical armadillo creature.
Gene Clark's spare, reflective solo album produced by Jesse Ed Davis.
First Yes album with Rick Wakeman, featuring Roundabout and Heart of the Sunrise.
Flute-led rock album critiquing organised religion and depicting a down-and-out title character.
Richard Perry-produced pop album featuring Without You, Coconut and Jump into the Fire.
Posthumously released album with the Full Tilt Boogie Band, including Me and Bobby McGee.
Includes Brown Sugar and Wild Horses, issued with a working-zipper Andy Warhol cover.
Synthesizer-laced hard rock salvaged from the Lifehouse project, featuring Baba O'Riley and Won't Get Fooled Again.
Marc Bolan's glam rock breakthrough, featuring Get It On and Jeepster.
First Yes album with Steve Howe, featuring Yours Is No Disgrace and Starship Trooper.
Orchestrated piano songs with Paul Buckmaster arrangements, including Tiny Dancer and Levon.
Polished album co-produced with Phil Spector, led by the idealistic title piano ballad.
Spare, confessional songs on dulcimer, piano and guitar, including A Case of You and River.
Lusher, jazz-tinged follow-up with brass, strings and guests including John Cale.
Concept album with Jean-Claude Vannier strings, choirs and prominent bass under Gainsbourg's half-spoken vocals.
Piano-led songs with Rick Wakeman, including Changes, Life on Mars? and Oh! You Pretty Things.
Opens with Eddie Hazel's ten-minute, grief-stricken guitar solo, followed by heavy psychedelic funk.
Darker, more intense Cohen record, including Famous Blue Raincoat and Avalanche.
Double album of locked-groove jams and tape experiments, with Damo Suzuki and Jaki Liebezeit's looping drums.
Song cycle on war, poverty and ecology, with layered vocals and flowing orchestral arrangements.
Final album with Jim Morrison, blues-based and loose, including Riders on the Storm.
Untitled album including Stairway to Heaven, Black Dog and When the Levee Breaks.
Triple album uniting the band with country and bluegrass elders like Maybelle Carter and Earl Scruggs.
Stomping, terrace-chant glam rock with Noddy Holder's roar, including Mama Weer All Crazee Now.
Jangling power pop debut from Alex Chilton and Chris Bell, including Thirteen and The Ballad of El Goodo.
Soundtrack whose sleek funk critiques the drug trade, including Freddie's Dead and Pusherman.
Sprawling double album recorded partly in a French villa basement, mixing blues, country, gospel and rock.
Debut mixing retro glamour and avant-garde noise, with Brian Eno's synthesizer treatments.
Double album from Minas Gerais musicians blending Brazilian folk, Beatles-style pop, jazz and rock.
Double album split into thematic sides spanning rock, country, bluegrass and Latin music.
David Bowie and Mick Ronson-produced album featuring Walk on the Wild Side and Perfect Day.
Norman Whitfield-produced album featuring the nearly twelve-minute Papa Was a Rollin' Stone.
Orchestrated, literary songs produced by Bernie Taupin, portraying American lives.
Debut of harmony-rich country rock, including Take It Easy and Witchy Woman.
Willie Mitchell-produced soul built on Al Green's falsetto, led by the title hit.
Tim Buckley's turn to sexually explicit, funky rock and soul with extended vocal improvisation.
Hugh Masekela's exile-era jazz session, blending South African melodies with flowing improvisation.
First post-Garfunkel solo album, mixing folk with reggae and Latin touches, including Mother and Child Reunion.
Live rock adaptation of Mussorgsky's piano suite, recorded at Newcastle City Hall.
Stark, brief album of solo voice and guitar, with a single piano overdub.
Randy Newman's satirical, orchestrated piano songs, including the title track and Political Science.
Double album largely played solo by Rundgren, including Hello It's Me and I Saw the Light.
Synthesizer-rich soul album, including Superstition and You Are the Sunshine of My Life.
Glam rock album featuring Metal Guru and Telegram Sam, produced by Tony Visconti.
Laid-back multiracial funk and Latin jazz, including The Cisco Kid and the title track.
Heavier Sabbath album recorded in Los Angeles, including Supernaut and the piano ballad Changes.
Country-tinged album recorded largely in Nashville, including Heart of Gold and Old Man.
Live double album from Osaka and Tokyo with extended versions of Highway Star and Smoke on the Water.
Theatrical hard rock with a West Side Story nod, led by the title anthem.
Debut of jazz-tinged pop rock, including Do It Again and Reelin' in the Years.
Three long tracks, with an 18-minute title suite inspired by Hermann Hesse's Siddhartha.
Recorded in Montreux with a mobile studio, including Smoke on the Water and Highway Star.
Concept album about an alien rock star, backed by Mick Ronson and the Spiders.
Theatrical Glasgow hard rock with Alex Harvey's dramatic vocals and a Jacques Brel title track.
Glam rock reflecting on fame and the band's struggles, including All the Way from Memphis.
Final Roxy album with Eno, including Do the Strand and the unsettling In Every Dream Home a Heartache.
Waylon Jennings sings Billy Joe Shaver songs, helping launch outlaw country's rougher sound.
Texas boogie and blues rock, including La Grange and Waitin' for the Bus.
Expanded Isleys lineup with Ernie Isley's fuzz guitar, featuring That Lady and soft-rock covers.
Island Records debut, overdubbed for rock audiences, including Concrete Jungle and Stir It Up.
